Now thereâs a better way to know whoâs who!
You visit a website. Your browser sends a request to the server and the server returns code for the browser to run.

The request already reveals information about you; what browser you use, the language itâs in, the OS that runs it and your IP address, which the server needs to send you the response. That often reveals your location.

See, weâve made a lot of civilizational progress in making browsing safe. Long gone are the days when getting a virus just by visiting a website was a daily concern. The thing is, the definition of safety varies depending on who you ask. The broad consensus ends at isolation: a websiteâs code canât see the data stored by other websites, and it canât see your files or other applications without permission. Chrome and Edge stop here. Then you have Safari (especially on iOS/macOS 26+) and Firefox extending that definition to privacy, but they still donât fully protect you from fingerprinting. Brave and Tor are the leading privacy-first browsers, with up and coming Mullvad Browser (Mullvad being, in my opinion, one of the best VPN providers out there).

The code runs on your hardware, which can be measured in ways that produce consistent and unique readings. Thereâs not much that can be done about this really, so thereâs only two established solutions:
- feed a little bit of noise here and there. Itâs called farbling and thatâs what Brave does to make your fingerprint inconsistent.
- make everything look the same, always, so thereâs no telling browser users apart. Tor and Mullvad adopt this approach.
So there are two sources for data that can make up your fingerprint; the network request and the code environment.
When you look at network, the data is generally either fragile or generic:

- the IP address; in a âhappy pathâ where one person always uses the same IP address, it might be the only data you need. But commonly people do a lot of browsing on mobile networks, they share the WiFi with others, they use VPNs or their home networkâs IP address is rotated by the ISP. Itâs fragile as such.
- headers like User-Agent orAccept-Language ; reveal your browser, OS, versions and the language set.
When you can execute code on the device, you have ways to measure its hardware qualities (without any permission prompts!) and these are surprisingly stable:
- CPU; behaviour, vendor, number of threads
- display data; resolution, pixel ratio, refresh rate
And on the software level; installed fonts, extensions, system infoâ¦
Millions of devices use the latest Chrome, there are millions of Macs with the M4 chip and there are millions of browsers in French.
But when you look at devices that run the latest Chrome in French on an M4, that number now drops significantly. Add to it hardware measurements and it gets so low it becomes practically unique.
The fingerprint doesnât need to be truly, globally unique - it just needs to be unique enough to tell people apart in your sample size.
A ZIP code (inferred from IP), a birth date (youâve given away on some platform) and sex (you fill it in everywhere) together are enough to uniquely identify over 60% of Americans.
You can always add another variable to decrease the potential pool of candidates.

Have you ever played Akinator? You think of a character, a genie asks you some twenty questions, and somehow it knows. Thatâs fingerprinting in a nutshell, except your browser answers the questions for you. Once you understand information entropy, Akinatorâs magic turns into a simple trick.

Letâs simplify with that game where you have to guess the character on a board through questions like âIs my character a man?â. If I say âyesâ, and half of the characters on your board are men, youâre now considering only half of the total candidates. Now we can say that my answer gave you logâ(100 / 50) = logâ(2) = 1 bit of information, because it cut the pool of candidates in half.
The bits you get from one answer are called its surprisal: the rarer the answer, the more it tells you.
- a trait shared by 1 in 2 people is worth 1 bit (is a man),
- 1 in 8 is worth 3 bits (has a mustache),
- and 1 in 128 is worth 7 bits (has one eye).
Surprisal quantifies the value of the answer, and entropy quantifies the value of the question. If 1 person in 128 is one-eyed, then asking about it will yield ânoâ 127 times in 128.
Summing up the contribution of each possible answer, the question itself is worth ~0.066 bits of entropy - thatâs the average amount of bits you gain from an answer.

When we combine traits that are independent we simply add up their bits or multiply the ratios, so a man with a mustache and one eye would mean 11 bits, or 1 in 2048. Alas, as Thomas Bayes would have you know, nothing is ever so simple in practice. A mustache is already a strong indicator of a man, and a man is probably more likely to have one eye. The traits are not independent so the bits donât really add up.
Some interesting applications of this type of reasoning:

- In medical diagnostics: A positive result from a 99% accurate test for a disease known to affect 0.01% of the population is about 100 times more likely to be wrong than you are to have the disease. You need more evidence!
- In cryptography: A password made out of four random words is as strong as eight random keyboard characters (but much easier to remember!)

- In forensic science: singling out one person in a city of a million takes about 20 bits. A witness description that matches 1 person in 1,000 provides only 10 bits, which still leaves a thousand possible suspects.
- coveryourtracks.eff.org shows you how unique your fingerprint is, with entropy for each measured data point.
If youâre using Chrome youâre basically walking around with an ID on your forehead.
Safari and Firefox offer some level of protection, but youâre still identifiable by advanced trackers.
Brave, Tor and Mullvad Browser are the only major browsers at the moment that implement advanced protections against fingerprinting.

If you donât feel like switching browsers, I get it. I am a big Arc fan myself and unfortunately itâs discontinued and will never have any privacy features. There are extensions like JShelter - they disrupt fingerprinting scripts by intercepting browser API calls. But they also break some websites. Same problem applies to Firefoxâs Resist Fingerprinting feature.

The ironic truth is, privacy extensions make you more unique, since fewer people have them. So a smart tracker could detect that, ignore the signals disrupted by the extension and focus on the ones that are not.
No extension can be as effective as engine-level protection built into the browser. So if you donât want to be tracked, you gotta commit.

Apple will announce a new smart home hub on Tuesday called the HomeView, according to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman.

Over the past couple of years, we’ve seen multiple reports that Apple was working on a new smart home product, but now it seems the product has a name and a launch date. Gurman described the HomeView as a Siri-powered device with a display and an A18 chip, allowing customers to control their other smart home devices.
The HomeView will reportedly be available in two models — one designed for countertops and the other to be mounted on walls.
This would be Apple’s most serious bet on the smart home to date, after it failed to get much traction for its HomeKit software framework or its HomePod smart speaker.

Gurman reports that on Tuesday, Apple will also be unveiling updated versions of two other home devices, namely the Apple TV set-top box and the HomePod mini. Earlier this week, he said that Apple plans to announce a partnership with LG to create a smart lock, a thermostat, and a doorbell.

The moment Trevor Wischnewsky heard that drones were delivering pizza and sushi around his Texas neighborhood, his mind was made up. “It was super fascinating,” he says. “I just immediately wanted to be a part of it.” Wischnewsky is now an RPIC, or “remote pilot in command,” at a company called FlyTrex. An RPIC is like an air traffic controller. But instead of airplanes, this new class of aviators tend to fleets of hexacopter drones that ferry cargo to homes and businesses within a three-mile radius. Not only does he ensure the safe passage of FlyTrex’s parcels, but Wischnewsky coordinates traffic with a growing swarm of delivery drones dotting the skies over Dallas from competitors like Zipline, Amazon, and Alphabet’s Wing. Here’s what it takes to land the gig.

When he applied to FlyTrex, Wischnewsky was in training to become a commercial pilot and flight instructor, and he was already certified by the Federal Aviation Administration as a drone pilot. The company requires this credential, along with a weeks-long FAA-approved training course, to ensure that a pilot is prepared to take over a drone if need be. Though he doesn’t pilot the craft, Wischnewsky monitors the delivery process from FlyTrex’s operations center with the help of inputs from GPS, lasers, and a range of sensors.

At first, the biggest challenge was trusting the technology. “On the manned-aircraft side, they tell you ‘Don’t trust the automation,’” Wischnewsky says. The Dallas–Fort Worth area, though, is a testing ground for unmanned aircraft systems traffic management (UTM), a network that allows autonomous drones from FlyTrex and its competitors to share their coordinates in real time to help avoid collisions even beyond the pilot’s line of sight. Once Wischnewsky makes sure a drone is flight-ready, its path is unimpeded, and the weather conditions are clear, UTM takes care of the rest.

At his busiest, Wischnewsky will have up to 10 drones on his watch at the same time. “You’re there as a safety net,” he says. Even with automation, keen situational awareness is required, and the most common hazard is the weather. Wischnewsky recalls a particularly stressful day: A drone had been in the air for only seconds when the wind picked up so suddenly that he had to intervene. He returned it safely, preventing an errant ice cream cake from hitting the sidewalk.
Eamon Whalen is a reporter and researcher based in San Francisco.

The other evening while biking home through the park I came upon a young woman sitting on a bench. I noticed her from a ways off because she was wearing a nice fall coat and looked like she was waiting for someone, and then as I was approaching, looking at her still, I watched her face light all the way up in a grin. I turned to see what she was reacting to, and it was a young guy approaching on a bike too, and when he saw her, his face lit up just like hers did. Two friends, or maybe more than friends, just so excited to see each other. I swear I could have wept.

Maybe I was so moved by the sight of them because of something I’d been ruminating about all day, a particular detail in the reporting of Jane Doe’s process of piecing together what happened to her on the night of October 19, 2024. A few days after the incident at Chi Phi, she learned that she’d been banned from the fraternity’s Halloween party, which she appeared to have planned to attend, perhaps in the hopes of repairing the damage that her reputation was undergoing as rumours about her were spreading. “Yall aren’t my friends,” she texted Matthew Ingalls, one of the alleged assailants with whom she had been exchanging conciliatory texts since the night of the incident. “Yall are covering your asses.”

Was Jane Doe wrong to have thought they were ever friends? What are bonds of friendship when sex is part of the mix? These questions have haunted me. Would real friendship have helped prevent the assault? What does real friendship between college-age men and women actually look like?

I have long thought of female friendship as a magical protection against pretty much everything bad that can happen to, or be enacted by, my sons. I don’t think girls are responsible for civilizing boys, but I do think that boys and girls who are comfortable together have an easier time, in general, moving through life. Friendship across genders is a skeleton key that makes the world feel less mysterious and hostile, but the tricky part is that you can’t force it to happen. I’ve been thinking lately about what inhibits friendship across genders and what encourages it.

It was easy when my sons were tiny: Toddlers will play with whomever they are plopped down next to, at least for a little while. As they got older, my friends and I continued to contrive opportunities for gender-agnostic hangs: a day trip to the apple orchard, a picnic at the park, a trip to the movies. It felt for a little while like we were creating a utopian environment for them — everyone all together, no questions asked. All the way through primary school, my sons hung out with girls pretty regularly.

By high school, though, the typical path for college-bound kids seems to lead to gender segregation. The enormous time demands of competitive sports are a big part of why this happens, but there’s also the generally wrenching process of status sorting in high school that both girls and boys endure, which tends to isolate them from each other except in certain contexts like homecoming (happy hoco to all who celebrate, by the way) and group projects at school.

There’s also the cumulative effect of social media, leading many boys and girls to speak in what are essentially different dialects. Some boys I know are so socialized into the world of streamers that they speak in a patois of memes and references that actively repels girls. Meanwhile most young women’s social feeds are heavily dedicated to beauty products, with a sprinkling of parsing the subtleties of problematic personalities and spotting green and red flags. Compatibility does not seem to be on anyone’s agenda. There emerges a sort of heteropessimism among preteens, and it seems to linger.

Recently on George Civeris and Sam Taggart’s excellent podcast, Straightiolab (dedicated to “unpacking the rich, multicolored tapestry of straight culture”), there was a discussion of the “boyfriend chair” that stores like Aritzia have outside the ladies’ changing rooms. The comic Ru Anderson, a guest on the show, remarked, “Why are you there? It’s like bringing a bad vibe to what’s supposed to be a positive shopping experience. The boyfriend is sitting, head down, on their phone. And it seems like the girlfriends don’t want them there either!”

“Here’s the really sad thing,” replies Civeris. “You think the Aritzia errand is a place where the man and the woman have nothing in common. What if I told you it’s one of the things that’s least dramatic for them to do together? Everything else they each want to do is actually even more alienating to the other partner. At the very least, the man can understand the concept of retail. And he can be like, Okay, we’re going to go there. She’s going to try on a few things. And I’m going to be like, ‘You look great, babe.’ And then we can move on. It’s so bleak. Think of the things that the man would be doing. Sports betting. He’s cheating on his girlfriend. He is online organizing a variety of paramilitary organizations with other men.”
Obviously this is comedy not anthropology, but they describe a dynamic we’ve all seen many times: a young couple enacting togetherness while seeming to occupy completely different worlds.

After an adolescence of gender isolation, everyone is thrown together in college and expected to interact like adults, comfortable with social norms and codes of behavior that are supposed to be equitable. Meanwhile sexual assault is a brutal fact of life almost everywhere. If kids’ social lives were less gender-segregated through high school, would this situation change for the better? To me, it’s an obvious conclusion.

High school and college should be prime time for making friends outside of your gender. That was certainly true for me. I’m lucky to count many straight men as friends today, but in every case, I’m also friends with their wives, and when we hang out, the women tend to pair off and talk about their own stuff. The last time I made friends with a man whose wife or girlfriend I wasn’t also friends with was before I had kids. Once the cogwheels of family life start turning, it gets harder to relate to each other across the gender divide. Grievances pile up, eyerolls, impatience. But in high school and college, we are blissfully ignorant of all ways our friendships can be undermined in the future. In that way, this era of friendship might be among the most important we’ll ever have. But it’s fragile.

The two young people in the park sent me back in time as I recalled the guy-friends of my past: housemates I’d eat midnight grilled cheese with, guys I studied with, guys I’d gone out for lunch with in high school, all of us piled in my friend Ryan’s enormous old Lincoln Continental. Guys like Liosha with whom I wrote an entire screenplay spoof of Forrest Gump when we were 13. Noah, whom I met freshman year of high school and whom I last saw just a few weeks ago, when he brought his parents to a book event I was doing.

A few days after I biked past the two in the park, I was interviewing dads about how they’re talking to their sons about Cornell. One of the many dads who replied to my callout on social media was a guy I’d been friends with in high school and hadn’t seen or heard from in 20 years. He’s married with four kids now, I learned. I called him up, and we ended up talking for over an hour, reminiscing, catching up about our families, comparing notes on kids and work and life. I had the sense that we are both basically the same people we were at 16, before all the responsibilities of life began to accumulate and shape our identities in new ways. This realization made me feel lighter than air.

The friendships we make across genders when we’re young help shape us, and these friends can demystify the world a little bit. They can prepare us for long-term relationships that aren’t based on fantasies, and they can help us break out of the prisons of gender itself by giving us rare access behind the scenes. Maybe most importantly though, they humanize us to each other. Jane Doe was mistaken in considering those guys her friends, but I hope there are other men in her life she can lean on if she wants to.

Fittingly, for a play that opens with a reenactment of Rodgers and Hammerstein’s Cinderella, Ryan J. Haddad’s Good Time Charlie is all about the valuable generational guide that is a fairy godparent. In this case, that’s Haddad’s uncle Charlie (played by a bubbling Jonathan Raviv), who is technically his father’s first cousin, but is also — crucially and non-derogatorily — very much a fairy. For many young gay men, the basic skills of life may come from immediate family, but along the way, someone has to swoop in to explain things that make it really worth living, teach you about Judy and Barbra and Little Edie and explain how to get into a sold-out Broadway show through the cancellation line. Given the facts of reproduction, most queer children aren’t born to queer parents, and so the intangible lessons hopscotch across generations like knights on a chessboard. Haddad, growing up in Shaker Heights, Ohio, needed someone to barge into his life like Auntie Mame. And if that Mame comparison sounds like a metaphor, it’s not. Under Danny Sharron’s happily indulgent direction, Raviv’s Charlie enters via staircase in a shiny vest early in the play singing half a verse of “It’s Today” before Haddad cuts him off. “We didn’t get the rights,” he announces.

As that scene suggests, Good Time Charlie develops into a warm, winking, sometimes sprawling tale of queer inheritance, a portrait of, by, and as an artist as a young gay man, by way of a portrait of another man who did not become an artist. The play’s tension, gently but poignantly unspooled, develops from the fact that while Ryan has pursued a career onstage, Charlie never did. In college, when Charlie suggested to his parents that he might switch majors to theater, they pushed him toward dentistry. When they discovered his sexuality, they tried to keep him in the closet. A generation later, Ryan has an easier — though not uncomplicated — experience coming out to the same family members, who are now more welcoming. The actors Nael Nacer and Artemis Pebdani double as Haddad’s great-aunt and -uncle and parents, playing across a spectrum of discomfort and cautious support. Nacer is quite good at variations of patriarchal obliviousness, and Pebdani suffuses her women with streaks of guilt. The casting gives the play’s repetitions a prismatic quality: pairs of parents fumbling to understand their sons, figures who appear cuddly from one angle revealed as sharp from another.

Along the way, Haddad also traces a lineage of lessons in the ephemeral aspects of queer culture, like what it means to choose your favorite actress and how much lube you might need during your freshman year in college. (Charlie sends Ryan six bottles, his parents are shocked to discover.) The play takes place in the Japanese-inspired garden, rendered in full bloom by set designer Afsoon Pajoufar, complete with a just-cheesy-enough big vermilion torii that’s tended by Charlie’s partner, Lou (Tim Bagley, emanating the same gentle warmth you might’ve seen him emit on Somebody Somewhere). Lou is himself 21 years older than Charlie and taught him, in turn, about gay culture after they met at a bar in Cleveland, where Charlie has been obliviously accepting drinks from men he didn’t intend to go out with. Lou’s close friend Sheldon (Michael Cristofer, occupying a lane somewhere between TCM host and Old Deuteronomy), a strongly opinionated classic-film buff, becomes a crucial part of the equation, too, as he and Charlie embark on cultural outings to New York while Sheldon stays in the garden. And because she herself would be slighted to be left out in the equation, let’s not forget Haddad’s “fabulous lesbian aunt,” Janice, who regularly reminds us that gay men take women like her for granted. (That she’s played by Fun Home’s Beth Malone adds a meta-layer to any of her lines about lesbians in musicals.)

In his work preceding Good Time Charlie, Haddad has dealt in similar forms of autobiography, often as a solo performer. He has cerebral palsy and uses a walker, and his work has focused on dating and disability, as in his breakout play, Hi, Are You Single?, a work of emotional and literal exhibitionism that is referenced in Charlie (he’d prefer some of his relatives not come see him strip down in it), as well as the more recent Hold Me in the Water and Dark Disabled Stories, which included stories from its other cast members. Good Time Charlie has Haddad shifting into a study of many characters at once and expanding in scale. The play, like a sturdy classic that Sheldon might love, runs over two hours with an intermission, not without dragging. Haddad has a showman’s sense of a good punch line — playing to his base here, he knows that an A Star Is Born or Grey Gardens: The Musical reference will kill — though his dialogue can be flatly presentational, and he is still feeling out what can be best expressed in action versus what can be summarized in narration. Caution is inevitable when presenting work about your own family. (The real Charlie is very much alive and saw the play in previews.) But Haddad and Sharron can verge toward the too gentle, adding caveats to painful moments with eddying bits of self-awareness, in which characters interrupt Haddad, insisting they don’t want to relive their own trauma, have rewrites. That’s a playwright’s wrestling match that, as my colleague Sara Holdren noted recently, doesn’t need an audience. Either give us that unflattering scene or don’t. You have to be willing to light the fuse of your Buddenbrooks or Long Day’s Journey Into Night, walk away, and live with the ensuing Thanksgiving-table explosions.

Not that Good Time Charlie is ever as brutal as Mann or O’Neill, and not that it needs to be. The Haddads are much lovelier people, it seems. The play is largely a study in kindness, in both form and subject — even while facing the tough inevitabilities of any life. A moving plotline, treated delicately in the second act, comes as Sheldon has a stroke and must start using a walker like Ryan, and as Ryan discovers his own hesitation and discomfort with another’s disability. This is a play full of people trying very hard to be there for each other and discovering what makes that difficult. Not everyone gets a godparent like Charlie, Lou, Sheldon, or Janice. A gay friend, after seeing the play, joked to me that it made him jealous — that he’d wished he’d had a flamboyant uncle or a cool butch aunt. I found myself tracing a pang around my own heart, too. I’ve had a very supportive family (a grandmother, for instance, who thought I was old enough at 9 to see Bernadette in Gypsy), but never such a close familial guide. Some people have all the luck, if not the rights to Mame.
Good Time Charlie is at the Public Theater through October 25.

Donald Trump has serious beef with every living former president. While the Bidens, Bushes, Clintons, and Obamas have made a big show of their post–White House chumminess, Trump’s vicious smears and elaborate conspiracy theories against his predecessors have left him excluded from the ex-presidents club. This isn’t all that surprising; Trump’s not one to put aside a good vendetta for the sake of national unity. What is remarkable, though, is that throughout his presidency, Trump has also been actively feuding with Abraham Lincoln.

This rivalry is obviously one-sided, as the 16th president has been dead for 161 years and is better than Trump by just about every measure. That actually seems to be the root of it: In Trump’s mind, Lincoln remains the one obvious exception to his claims of being the greatest president of all time.
“I’ve always said I can be more presidential than any president in history,” Trump said in 2019. “Except for Honest Abe Lincoln when he’s wearing the hat.”

Trump talks about Lincoln like he’s a Republican frenemy who might dare to challenge him in the next election, not a long-dead, widely revered historical figure. Though the current president often makes a show of paying homage to “Honest Abe,” Trump regularly lashes out at him too. Trump has disparaged Lincoln’s (nonexistent) poll numbers, downplayed the importance of the 13th Amendment, and blasted his predecessor for not using Art of the Deal tactics to prevent the Civil War.
Here’s a guide to all of Trump’s bizarre attempts to wrap himself in Lincoln’s glory while subtly taking down the “Great Unifier.”
I’ll ‘heal the divisions’ like Lincoln … starting by suing my accusers.
During a 2016 speech at what he called the “hallowed ground” of Gettysburg, Pennsylvania, then-candidate Trump claimed that, if elected, he would look to unify the nation like the 16th president.

“President Lincoln served at a time of division like we’ve never seen before,” he said. “It is my hope that we can look to his example to heal the divisions we are living through right now. We are a very divided nation.”

Then, just like Honest Abe, Trump slammed the “totally rigged” political system, attacked the media for misreporting his crowd size, and said of his many sexual-assault accusers, “All of these liars will be sued after the election is over.”
‘I don’t know if it’s ever been done before.’
The night before his first inauguration, Trump held a concert at the Lincoln Memorial. He gave Abe a vigorous salute, then started bragging about his own historic achievements.

“This started out tonight being a small little concert, and then we had the idea, Maybe we will do it in front of the Lincoln Memorial,” he said. “I don’t know if it’s ever been done before, but if it has, very seldom. And the people came by the thousands and thousands.”
There have actually been a good number of historic musical performances at the national monument. But sure, no other president has serenaded Abe with the Rolling Stones’ “Heart of Stone.”
‘I can be more presidential than any president’ … except Lincoln.
At a rally in Youngstown, Ohio, Trump shouted that he was more presidential than nearly all of his predecessors.

“It is much easier to act presidential than what we are doing here tonight, believe me,” Trump assured his audience. “With the exception of the late, great Abraham Lincoln, I can be more presidential than any president that’s ever held this office.”
In the summer of 2018, Trump started referring to a “new poll” that had him “over 90 percent,” making him “the most popular Republican in history of the Party.”

During a trip to the U.K., the president bragged about this to The Sun, saying, “You know, a poll just came out that I am the most popular person in the history of the Republican Party. Beating Lincoln. I beat our Honest Abe.”
A few weeks later, even Trump seemed doubtful — with good reason. There were no polls in the 1860s, and we never got to the bottom of what survey he was referencing.

‘I believe I am treated worse’ than Lincoln.

“I am greeted with a hostile press, the likes of which no president has ever seen. The closest would be that gentleman right up there,” Trump said, pointing to the marble statue of Lincoln behind him.
“They always said, ‘Lincoln, nobody got treated worse than Lincoln,’” Trump continued. “I believe I am treated worse.”
‘I’ve done more for the Black community than any president,’ except (possibly) Lincoln.
Up to this point, Trump’s comparisons to Lincoln were largely silly and subjective. Then, in June 2020, he got into a one-sided fight with Abe over which of them had done more for Black Americans.
Initially, Trump exempted Lincoln from comments suggesting his policies, such as the First Step Act, were more significant than enforcing Brown v. Board of Education or passing the Civil Rights Act.

Trump replied, “But we are free. You understand what I mean. So I’m gonna take a pass on Abe — Honest Abe, as we call him.”
People didn’t know Lincoln was a Republican ‘until I came along.’
A few months into his presidency, Trump said of Lincoln, “Most people don’t even know he was a Republican.”
Three years later, Trump gave himself credit for preserving this arcane bit of Lincoln lore.

During a rally in Pennsylvania, Trump dropped a greatest-hits album of his Lincoln commentary with a new bonus track.

“You know we’re the party of Abraham Lincoln, a lot of people don’t know that,” Trump said. “The great Abraham Lincoln, a man that I’ve always competed against. ‘This is Donald Trump, hopefully your favorite president of all time, better than Lincoln, better than Washington.’

Did Lincoln willfully ignore the lessons of The Art of the Deal because he wanted to secure his legacy? Well, Trump insinuates, you decide!

“Abraham Lincoln, of course, if he negotiated it, you probably wouldn’t even know who Abraham Lincoln was,” Trump said. “He would’ve been president, but he would’ve been president, and he would have been — he wouldn’t have been the Abraham Lincoln.”
During a rally in Pennsylvania, Trump called Gettysburg, the bloodiest battle of the Civil War, “vicious and horrible” yet “beautiful in so many ways.”
Then he lamented that Confederate General Robert E. Lee is “no longer in favor” and recalled his famous directive “Never fight uphill, me boys” — which Lee never said.
This wasn’t directly about Lincoln, but it does feel like Trump was trying to one-up the former president by including a pirate impression in his Gettysburg Address.
I’m ‘tougher on the border’ than Lincoln.

While bragging about receiving the endorsement of a Border Patrol union at a North Carolina rally, Trump claimed a group official told him he’s the “greatest president there’s ever been,” even better than Washington or Lincoln.
“He said I’m tougher on the border than Abraham Lincoln, right, than Honest Abe,” Trump added.
A gaudy marble bathroom is ‘appropriate for the time of Abraham Lincoln.’

Trump gutted the White House’s Lincoln Bathroom, then claimed the floor-to-ceiling marble was accurate to the 1860s. But the real Lincoln used an outhouse before he came to Washington. And he was furious when his wife overspent on White House renovations, saying she’d wasted money on “flub dubs for this damned old house.”

Trump posts a lot of weird AI-generated art on Truth Social (the image of him escorting a swole, handcuffed alien around a military base comes to mind). During the summer, he repeatedly shared this shot of himself hanging with (imaginary) rivals Washington and Lincoln with no commentary.
‘Donald J. Trump is six times more popular than Abraham Lincoln.’

In November 2020, a freak wave appeared, lifting a lone buoy off the coast of British Columbia 17.6 meters (58 feet) high.
A few years later, the four-story wall of water was confirmed to be the most extreme rogue wave ever recorded.
Such an extraordinary event is thought to happen only once every 1,300 years.
And if the buoy hadn't been taken for a ride, we might never have known it had occurred.
For centuries, rogue waves were regarded as mere nautical folklore.

It wasn't until 1995 that myth became reality. On the first day of the new year, a nearly 26-meter (85-foot) wave struck an oil-drilling platform about 160 kilometers (100 miles) off the coast of Norway.
At the time, the so-called Draupner wave defied all previous models scientists had put together.

Since then, dozens more rogue waves have been recorded (some even in lakes), and while the one that surfaced near Ucluelet, Vancouver Island was not the tallest, its relative size compared to the waves around it was unprecedented.
Scientists define a rogue wave as any wave more than twice the height of the waves surrounding it. The Draupner wave, for instance, was 25.6 meters tall, while its neighbors were only 12 meters tall.
In comparison, the Ucluelet wave was nearly three times the size of its peers.
"Proportionally, the Ucluelet wave is likely the most extreme rogue wave ever recorded," explained physicist Johannes Gemmrich from the University of Victoria in 2022.
"Only a few rogue waves in high sea states have been observed directly, and nothing of this magnitude."

Today, researchers are still trying to figure out how rogue waves are formed so we can better predict when they will arise. This includes measuring rogue waves in real time and also running models on the way they get whipped up by the wind.
The buoy that picked up the Ucluelet wave was placed offshore, along with dozens of others, by a research institute called MarineLabs in an attempt to learn more about hazards out in the deep.
"The unpredictability of rogue waves, and the sheer power of these 'walls of water' can make them incredibly dangerous to marine operations and the public," said MarineLabs CEO Scott Beatty.
"The potential of predicting rogue waves remains an open question, but our data is helping to better understand when, where, and how rogue waves form, and the risks that they pose."
Even when freak waves occur far offshore, they can still destroy marine operations, wind farms, or oil rigs. If they are big enough, they can even put the lives of beachgoers at risk.
Luckily, neither Ucluelet nor Draupner caused any severe damage or took any lives, but other rogue waves have.
Some ships that went missing in the 1970s, for instance, are now thought to have been sunk by sudden, looming waves.
The floating wreckage left behind looks like the work of an immense white cap.

Unfortunately, a 2020 study predicted that wave heights in the North Pacific will increase with climate change, suggesting the Ucluelet wave may not hold its record for as long as our current predictions suggest.
Experimental research published in 2024 suggests these monstrous waves can be up to four times higher than previously thought possible.
"We are aiming to improve safety and decision-making for marine operations and coastal communities through widespread measurement of the world's coastlines," said MarineLabs CEO Scott Beatty.
"Capturing this once-in-a-millennium wave, right in our backyard, is a thrilling indicator of the power of coastal intelligence to transform marine safety."

The effort to predict rogue waves got a boost in February 2026, when a team led by researchers from the University of South Florida published a new analysis in Ocean Science, testing years of real buoy data against the global wave models scientists currently rely on to forecast ocean conditions.
The team found those models consistently underestimate just how extreme waves can get, missing much of the long tail of rare, towering waves that buoys actually pick up in the real world.
Rogue waves turned out to be far from random, too.

They peaked in winter and clustered most heavily off the US West Coast, with the North Atlantic a close second – putting the Pacific Northwest, where the Ucluelet wave struck, squarely in the highest-risk zone.

The researchers also flagged a possible early-warning sign buried in the data.

In roughly three-quarters of the rogue waves they examined, a sharp dip in wave correlation was followed by a rapid rebound right before the wave hit – a pattern they hope could eventually feed into real-time forecasting tools.
The study on the Ucluelet wave was published in Scientific Reports.
The Air Force has figured out a way for maintainers to inspect what had been a “blind spot” in F-16 engines, after problems in that area led to the catastrophic crashes of two jets in recent years.
A spokesperson for the Air Force Life Cycle Management Center confirmed the new procedure to Air & Space Forces Magazine last month. Task & Purpose first reported the development.

AFLCMC’s propulsion directorate developed the new process, which does not require any modifications to the engine or new equipment, the spokesperson added. The inspections is meant specifically for Pratt & Whitney F100 engine models—some F-16s are powered by GE Aerospace F110 models.

The F100 engine consists of 13 “stages,” each with variable vanes and compressor blades. Air flows through the stages, which rotate to accelerate, compress, and then regulate the airflow before releasing it into the engine’s combustion chamber. If a vane is turned or misaligned, however, it creates “abnormal aerodynamic forces” and “irregular wake patterns” that put stress on the compressor blades in the following stages, according to Air Force reports. That can lead to vanes or blades cracking or breaking, causing the entire engine to fail.

Maintainers can inspect many of the F100 engine’s stages using a borescope—a camera mounted on a flexible tube. There are even borescope ports for them to do so. But the fourth and especially the fifth stages are hard to reach. Before the development of this new inspection process, the Air Force said it was impossible for maintainers to inspect them without completely disassembling the engine, something only done at depots and not while the engine is installed on the aircraft.

This blind spot proved dangerous. An F-16 crashed near Holloman Air Force Base, N.M., in April 2024, and another jet, belonging to the U.S. Air Force Thunderbirds, crashed in the California desert in December 2025. Subsequent investigations determined that in both cases, the F-16s’ engines had failed because of misaligned vanes in the fifth stage.
The pilots in both crashes were able to safely eject, but both jets were completely destroyed and the total damages exceeded $54 million.

Notably, both F-16 engines in question had experienced foreign object debris, or FOD, events in the years prior to the crashes. In both cases, maintainers noted damage to early stages of the inlet fan but found no issues with the fourth, seventh, or eighth stages—and the F-16’s technical orders did not require maintainers to remove and disassemble the engine core to inspect the fifth and sixth stages after a FOD event if no damage is found in the surrounding stages.

While investigators were unable to conclusively say if the FOD events led to the vanes becoming misaligned, the Air Force has now updated its technical orders to require the new inspection procedure to check the fifth stage of the engine after every FOD event.

“Additionally, the program office has worked with Pratt & Whitney to redesign the vane arm to be more impact resistant. The new design is qualified, on order, and will be installed via forced retrofit as soon as available,” the AFLCMC spokesperson said.

SpaceX and NASA are preparing to send the next crew of four to the International Space Station as soon as Thursday morning, weather permitting.
The mission, NASA’s SpaceX Crew-13, is led by NASA astronaut Jessica Watkins, who will become the first agency astronaut to fly twice onboard a SpaceX Dragon spacecraft.

She along with NASA Astronaut Luke Delaney, Canadian Space Agency (CSA) astronaut Joshua Kutryk, and Roscosmos cosmonaut Sergey Teteryatnikov, will fly onboard Dragon Grace to the ISS for a six-month expedition.

Liftoff of the Falcon 9 rocket from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station is scheduled for 11:10 a.m. EDT (1510 UTC). The rocket will fly on a north-easterly trajectory upon leaving the pad. Docking is scheduled to occur about eight hours after launch, the shortest transit time ever for a Dragon spacecraft.
Spaceflight Now will have live coverage about four hours prior to liftoff.
The 45th Weather Squadron forecast a 55 percent chance for acceptable weather at launch. Meteorologists are watching for the potential interference from clouds and rain at the pad.

“Over the next 24 hours, a weak low-level disturbance sliding along the south side of the high into the Gulf will bring breezy onshore flow that will continue into the primary launch window late Thursday morning,” launch weather officers wrote on Wednesday.
“Models still suggest the continued threat for onshore moving Atlantic showers along the coast, with the exact timing and locations of this activity the main forecast challenge.”

SpaceX will launch the mission using the Falcon 9 first stage booster with the tail number B1101. This will be its third flight after previously launching 29 Starlink V2 Mini satellites on the Starlink 6-88 mission and Dragon Freedom on NASA’s SpaceX Crew-12.

Less than eight minutes after liftoff, B1101 will return to Cape Canaveral and target a touchdown at Landing Zone 40 (LZ-40). If all goes well, this will be the seventh landing at LZ-40 and the 664th Falcon booster landing to date.
The Crew-13 mission is the second trip to space for Commander Jessica Watkins who previously served as a mission specialist on the Crew-4 mission, which flew in 2022.

Watkins, a geologist and avid athlete, spent her time in between missions working as a branch chief within the Astronaut Office and later, did some work in support of the crewed rovers and spacesuits needed for future Moon-bound missions within the Artemis Program.

“I certainly would ideally like to be a servant leader. I think that is something that I have learned through my experiences, but also my interactions with leaders that I look up to and that I want to emulate,” Watkins said. “And that has come in the form of coaches, of mentors, of teachers, and of my crewmates and classmates as well here at NASA.”

At her side in the pilot’s seat is a former test pilot Luke Delaney. Before being selected as a member of the 2021 astronaut class, he worked as a research pilot and aerospace engineer at NASA’s Langley Research Center in Virginia.
Delaney grew up in Central Florida and said watching the space shuttle launches was a big inspiration for him and helped influence his life’s trajectory.

“Growing up watching shuttle launches, they weren’t quite as frequent back then, so it was a pretty big deal if you’re able to catch a space shuttle launch. And they definitely played a part in driving me towards both engineering background a little bit, plus aviation and those kind of things,” Delaney said.

“I think it’s just when you’re little and you see something like that and you’re trying to reconcile that there’s humans on that vehicle and they’re going to go live in space for a little bit and come back, that’s just a huge motivation, inspiration, however you want to put it. So for me, yeah, that was a big pinnacle aspect of going down that track for an astronaut.”

Another member of the crew who dreamed of becoming an astronaut ever since childhood is one of the two mission specialists, Joshua Kutryk. He becomes the second Canadian to fly to space in 2026 after Jeremy Hansen flew with the Artemis 2 crew.
The last Canadian who served onboard the space station was David Saint-Jacques who launched in December 2018 and returned to earth in June 2019.

Kutryk, who was selected by CSA to train as an astronaut in 2017, was previously assigned to the Boeing Starliner-1 mission, but that flight was altered to a cargo-only mission following the significant issues that arose throughout the Starliner Crew Flight Test mission.

“Excited because it’s been a long time, dreamt about my whole life. Been training for it for a lot of years, a lot of years, and you know about the Starliner history because we talked about it last time,” Kutryk told Spaceflight Now this summer. “So for all those reasons, really excited to have it this close. And then also, I think we all, all four of us would say this, we feel proud to be representing our nations, our agencies to be trusted and given the opportunity to do this.”

“Behind me lay all I held dear in life. And what lay before me? Happy child, little do you know what life is — how strangely mingled and how full of change… and now, a farewell to home. It was the darkest hour of the whole journey.” pic.twitter.com/iQOy9G9d9Y
— Joshua Kutryk (@Astro_Kutryk) September 30, 2026
The other mission specialist is Russian cosmonaut Sergey Teteryatnikov. He was selected for cosmonaut training by Roscosmos in 2021 and became a test cosmonaut two years later.
He said it was a chance meeting that put him on the path that will soon take him to space.

“In the course of my career, at some point, I had a meeting with a cosmonaut, those are regularly held. And I was told that actually there is an open contest, and one can try to become a cosmonaut, which I did when I was 30 years old,” Teteryatnikov said through the aid of a translator. “And that’s how it all started, and I started my cosmonaut training in 2021.”

The crew will join the other members of Expedition 75 on the space station. After a handover period of a few days, the members of the SpaceX Crew-12 mission will board Dragon Freedom to head back home.

NASA announced Wednesday a mission to explore the history and evolution of the universe, PRIMA (PRobe far-Infrared Mission for Astrophysics), is advancing to the next phase of development. This space telescope is the first in a new class of NASA astrophysics missions, called Probe Explorers, within the agency’s longstanding Explorers Program.

“The PRIMA mission is humanity’s next window into the deep universe. It will unveil the obscure across cosmic time to better understand the formation of planets, stars, black holes, and even how water on Earth came to be,” said Nicky Fox, associate administrator, Science Mission Directorate, NASA Headquarters in Washington.

NASA selected PRIMA to move into Phase B, the stage of development that advances the preliminary design and technology development for the mission. The mission is subject to a confirmation review, based on technical, programmatic, and cost performance, to determine its readiness to begin implementation in Phase C. If confirmed, PRIMA’s project cost is capped at $1.2 billion, not including launch and other non-project costs. The observatory will be targeted to launch in 2033, for a planned five-year mission.

With a 5.9-foot telescope, PRIMA will conduct deep, sensitive surveys of the universe in far-infrared light, helping bridge the gap between existing infrared observatories, such as NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope, and radio telescopes. By studying radiant energy that only emerges in the far-infrared, PRIMA will address a wide range of questions about the universe. This includes the origins of planets outside our solar system, how galaxies and their black holes have grown and evolved over cosmic history, and how dust and heavy elements have built up in the universe over time — all helping paint a better picture of why the universe looks the way it does today.

“A single mission alone can’t probe all the universe’s mysteries. But by extending the survey capabilities of our fleet into far-infrared wavelengths with PRIMA, we’re enabling an incredibly comprehensive look at the cosmos,” said Shawn Domagal-Goldman, director, Astrophysics Division, NASA Headquarters. “With our Webb and Roman space telescopes, we set a cadence of launching premiere-class missions in both halves of the decade. We’re going to keep that up and kick off the next decade with PRIMA, as part of a pipeline that will consistently have missions of this caliber ready to go.”

The National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine’s 2020 Decadal Survey, Pathways to Discovery in Astronomy and Astrophysics for the 2020s, recommended NASA establish this new Probe Explorers mission class. NASA selected PRIMA for development after detailed evaluation of concept studies for Probe Explorer missions, based on their scientific merit in alignment with the Decadal Survey’s recommendations, feasibility of their development plans on cost and schedule, and use of technologies that could support the development of future large missions.

NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California will manage the PRIMA mission. Other partners include NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland and NASA’s Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama. The PRIMA mission will also have contributions from international partners: CNES (Centre National D'Etudes Spatiales), ASI (Agenzia Spaziale Italiana), DLR (Deutsches Zentrum für Luft- und Raumfahrt), CSA (the Canadian Space Agency), KASI (Korea Astronomy and Space Science Institute)/KASA (Korea AeroSpace Administration), JAXA (Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency), and UKSA (the UK Space Agency).

The Explorers Program is the oldest continuous NASA program designed to provide frequent, low-cost access to space using principal investigator-led space science investigations relevant to the Science Mission Directorate’s astrophysics and heliophysics programs. Since the Explorer 1 launch in 1958, which discovered Earth’s radiation belts, the Explorers Program has launched more than 100 missions, including the Uhuru and Cosmic Background Explorer missions that led to Nobel prizes for their investigators.

The Explorers Program is managed by NASA Goddard for the Science Mission Directorate, which conducts a wide variety of research and scientific exploration programs for Earth studies, space weather, the solar system, and the universe.

A journalist stripped of her Indonesian citizenship in 1965 comes home decades later to children who grew up without her in “Casparina,” the second feature from actor-director Reza Rahadian, inspired by the life of his grandmother Francisca Casparina Fanggidaej.

In the film, Rina is driven into exile for opposing the government. Thirty-four years on, a letter tells her the old regime has collapsed and she is free to come home. Torn, she goes back to her children Andi and Lila, now grown and settled into lives that never included her. As she works through their hurt and resentment over the years she was gone, mother and children slowly find their way back to each other, and they come to understand what she gave up for her country and her family.

Rahadian says he was drawn to a story of motherhood told through children whose mother was missing from their lives, set in a moment when a person’s citizenship could be taken away suddenly, by force and without warning. The separation, he says, kept his grandmother and her children apart for 32 years. “This is for me a very important story,” he says.

He hopes viewers come away understanding that hard choices carry a price, and that they are sometimes driven by forces a person cannot see. He also wants audiences to grasp, in his words, “what it means to be a mother that is absent for 32 years,” and what it meant for her children to be unable to say openly who their mother was, because doing so could have put their lives at risk.

Producers Arya Ibrahim and Gita Fara describe the project as a story of the political upheaval of 1965, which tore families apart and left people who lost their citizenship living as exiles. According to the producers, Casparina was in Beijing representing Indonesia at an international forum when her citizenship was revoked over her opposition to the new regime. She left six children behind and spent 32 years in exile, first in Beijing and later in the Netherlands, before the family reconnected.
For the producers, stories like hers explain much about Indonesian history and identity. They call Casparina “a victim of an era” and see the film as a reminder not to repeat the same mistakes.
Rahadian’s first feature as director, “On Your Lap,” won four prizes at the Busan festival’s Vision awards in 2025, including the audience award and the Fipresci award.
“Casparina” is in the early stages of scriptwriting. In Busan, the producers hope to meet potential partners and collaborators, film funds and co-production opportunities.
A surprisingly simple way to relieve knee arthritis pain without pills or surgery
A simple change in how you walk could ease knee arthritis pain as effectively as medication while helping protect cartilage from further damage.

- A surprisingly simple change in how you walk could help relieve knee arthritis pain and even slow joint damage. In a year-long clinical trial, researchers found that adjusting the angle of a person's foot while walking reduced osteoarthritis pain by an amount comparable to medication, without requiring drugs or surgery. Even more promising, MRI scans revealed that participants who adopted the personalized walking technique experienced slower deterioration in a marker of knee cartilage health.
What if easing knee arthritis pain did not require another pill, an injection, or surgery, but simply changing how you walk?

A clinical trial published in The Lancet Rheumatology suggests that a small, carefully chosen adjustment to the angle of your feet could make a meaningful difference. After one year, participants who learned to walk with a personalized foot position reported significantly less knee pain than those receiving a placebo treatment. They also showed encouraging signs of slower deterioration in their knee cartilage.

The pain relief was comparable in magnitude to benefits reported for some commonly used medications. More importantly, the approach may help address something painkillers cannot: the excessive pressure on knee joints that contributes to osteoarthritis progression.
A Simple Walking Change Could Help Fight Knee Arthritis

Osteoarthritis affects roughly 22% of adults over age 40 and is one of the leading causes of disability. The condition gradually damages cartilage, the smooth, protective tissue that cushions the ends of bones and allows joints to move with minimal friction.

As cartilage deteriorates, everyday activities such as walking, climbing stairs, and getting out of a chair can become increasingly painful. Although exercise, physical therapy, weight management, and medications can help manage symptoms, there is currently no established treatment that reliably restores cartilage lost to osteoarthritis. People with advanced disease may eventually need joint replacement surgery.

Researchers from the University of Utah, New York University, and Stanford University have investigated a different strategy called gait retraining. Rather than focusing only on relieving pain, this approach changes the mechanics of walking to reduce pressure on vulnerable parts of the knee.

The findings, published in August 2025, came from the first randomized, placebo-controlled clinical trial to demonstrate the effectiveness of personalized gait retraining for knee osteoarthritis over a full year.

The research was co-led by Scott Uhlrich, an assistant professor of mechanical engineering at the University of Utah's John and Marcia Price College of Engineering, with collaborators at Stanford and New York University. The work received support from federal research agencies, with the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs listed as the trial's funder.

"We've known that for people with osteoarthritis, higher loads in their knee accelerate progression, and that changing the foot angle can reduce knee load," said Uhlrich, an assistant professor of mechanical engineering. "So the idea of a biomechanical intervention is not new, but there have not been randomized, placebo-controlled studies to show that they're effective."
The secret lies in how body weight moves through the knee with each step.

The knee has an inner section, called the medial compartment, and an outer section, known as the lateral compartment. During normal walking, the inner section typically carries more of the load. This helps explain why osteoarthritis affecting the inside of the knee is especially common.
For people with this type of arthritis, repeatedly placing excessive pressure on the already damaged area can accelerate deterioration.

Changing the direction in which the toes point during walking can redistribute some of that pressure. Turning the toes slightly inward or outward alters the forces acting on the knee, potentially reducing stress on the affected cartilage.
However, there is an important catch: the same adjustment does not work for everyone.

Some people benefit from turning their toes inward, while others respond better when their toes point farther outward. Making the wrong adjustment could fail to help or even increase pressure on the damaged joint.

"Previous trials prescribed the same intervention to all individuals, resulting in some individuals not reducing, or even increasing, their joint loading," Uhlrich said. "We used a personalized approach to selecting each individual's new walking pattern, which improved how much individuals could offload their knee and likely contributed to the positive effect on pain and cartilage that we saw."
How Scientists Found the Right Walking Pattern
The researchers focused on people with mild to moderate osteoarthritis affecting the inner part of the knee.

At their first two laboratory visits, participants underwent MRI scans and walked on a specialized treadmill equipped with sensors that measured the forces generated during each step. Motion capture cameras recorded their movements in detail, allowing the researchers to analyze how different walking styles affected the knee.
Participants tested small changes in their foot position, turning their toes inward or outward by either 5° or 10°.
The scientists then identified which adjustment reduced pressure on the affected knee most effectively for each person.

Not everyone qualified. Some prospective participants were excluded because none of the tested adjustments successfully reduced their knee loading. Including such individuals in earlier studies may help explain why previous attempts at gait retraining produced inconsistent results.
After the initial assessments, 68 participants were randomly divided into two groups of 34.

One group received personalized instructions designed to minimize stress on the inner knee. The other received a sham treatment, meaning they went through the same training process but were instructed to maintain their natural foot angle.

This comparison allowed the researchers to separate the benefits of changing walking mechanics from improvements caused by expectations, attention from researchers, or participation in a structured walking program.
Just Six Weeks of Training Changed How They Walked
Both groups attended six weekly training sessions.

During these visits, participants walked on a treadmill while wearing a small device on their shin. The device provided biofeedback, delivering gentle vibrations whenever their foot moved outside the prescribed angle.
Biofeedback is a technique that uses immediate signals to help people recognize and gradually control movements they normally perform without thinking.
Over time, participants learned to maintain their assigned foot position without needing constant reminders.
After completing the six weeks of supervised training, they were encouraged to practice their walking technique for at least 20 minutes each day until it became a natural habit.
Follow-up assessments indicated that participants were remarkably consistent. On average, they maintained their prescribed foot angles to within approximately one degree.
That consistency is important because the potential benefits depend on continuing the altered walking pattern during ordinary daily activities, not just during laboratory sessions.
Arthritis Pain Improved, and Cartilage Showed Less Damage
One year after starting the program, participants returned for another MRI and reported how much knee pain they were experiencing.
The results showed a meaningful advantage for those who received personalized gait retraining.
On a pain scale from zero to 10, participants in the intervention group reported an average improvement of 2.5 points, compared with 1.3 points in the sham group.
In an exploratory analysis, approximately 91% of participants receiving personalized retraining experienced a clinically meaningful reduction in pain, compared with 66% in the comparison group.

The researchers also found that the intervention reduced a mechanical measure associated with pressure on the inner knee, confirming that the altered walking pattern had effects beyond participants' perceptions of pain.

"The reported decrease in pain over the placebo group was somewhere between what you'd expect from an over-the-counter medication, like ibuprofen, and a narcotic, like OxyContin," Uhlrich said. "With the MRIs, we also saw slower degradation of a marker of cartilage health in the intervention group, which was quite exciting."
The MRI findings may be especially important.
Researchers used advanced imaging techniques capable of detecting subtle changes in cartilage composition before major structural damage becomes visible on conventional scans.

One measurement, known as T1rho, suggested that cartilage in the inner knee deteriorated more slowly among participants who changed their walking pattern. A second MRI measurement did not show a significant difference between the groups.

These findings do not establish that damaged cartilage was rebuilt or that arthritis progression can be permanently stopped. However, they raise the possibility that reducing mechanical stress could help preserve cartilage health over time.

The treatment also appeared generally well tolerated. No severe adverse events were reported, although two participants in the intervention group and one in the sham group withdrew because of increased knee pain.
More Recent Research Adds to the Evidence
Research published since the 2025 trial has provided further insight into how walking modifications might help people with knee osteoarthritis.

In a separate randomized trial published in Clinical Biomechanics in April 2026, researchers at the University of Bath investigated different types of biofeedback training in 50 people with knee osteoarthritis.
Participants completed a six-week program using different feedback strategies intended to improve walking mechanics.

All three groups, including the control group, experienced improvements in activity-related knee pain and physical function. However, only the group receiving feedback about its walking pattern achieved a lasting reduction in a key measure of knee loading.
That group's knee loading measure fell by 7.6%, with the improvement maintained at a follow-up assessment one month later.

Interestingly, the investigators did not detect significant changes in foot angle in any of the groups. This suggests that other adjustments to walking mechanics can also influence the forces acting on the knee.

The findings reinforce an important lesson from the 2025 trial: simply encouraging people to walk differently is not necessarily enough. The type of movement being taught, and whether it successfully reduces harmful joint loading, appears to matter.
The 2026 study did not examine long-term cartilage deterioration, so it cannot establish whether these additional walking strategies slow osteoarthritis progression.
Could This Help People Avoid Knee Replacement?
For people living with knee osteoarthritis, the appeal of this approach extends beyond its measurable effects in the laboratory.
One trial participant described the freedom of adopting a treatment that did not require medication or an assistive device:
"I don't have to take a drug or wear a device…it's just a part of my body now that will be with me for the rest of my days, so that I'm thrilled with."
Once a person learns the technique, it can potentially become part of ordinary daily movement without requiring continued use of specialized equipment.
That could be particularly valuable for people who develop arthritis relatively early in adulthood.

"Especially for people in their 30s, 40s, or 50s, osteoarthritis could mean decades of pain management before they're recommended for a joint replacement," Uhlrich said. "This intervention could help fill that large treatment gap."

Whether gait retraining can actually delay or prevent knee replacement remains unknown. Longer studies would need to demonstrate that its benefits persist and translate into better joint health and fewer surgical procedures.
Still, the prospect of relieving pain while potentially slowing cartilage deterioration makes personalized walking adjustments an intriguing addition to the available treatment options.
Smart Shoes and Smartphone Cameras Could Make Treatment Easier
One major obstacle remains: delivering personalized gait retraining outside a specialized research laboratory.

The original trial relied on sophisticated motion capture equipment, pressure-sensitive treadmill measurements, MRI scans, and repeated in-person visits. Those resources are expensive and difficult to provide in ordinary physical therapy clinics.
Researchers are exploring ways to make the technology much simpler.

"We and others have developed technology that could be used to both personalize and deliver this intervention in a clinical setting using mobile sensors, like smartphone video and a 'smart shoe'," Uhlrich said.

Smartphone cameras could help analyze walking mechanics and estimate how different movements influence knee loading. Meanwhile, shoes fitted with motion sensors could provide feedback as patients practice walking at home or around their neighborhoods.

Work published in Machine Learning with Applications in September 2026 explored another possibility: using artificial intelligence to estimate knee loading from acceleration measurements collected at the foot.

In that proof of concept study, researchers analyzed walking data from 10 healthy adults and demonstrated that a machine learning system could track changes in estimated knee forces across different walking patterns.

The technology remains experimental and has not yet been validated as a treatment tool for people with knee osteoarthritis. Nevertheless, it illustrates how future rehabilitation systems might provide personalized guidance without requiring a room full of cameras and laboratory equipment.
A Promising Treatment, but Not a Do-It-Yourself Fix
Despite the encouraging results, researchers caution that personalized gait retraining is not yet ready for widespread clinical use.

The original study included only 68 participants, all of whom had mild to moderate osteoarthritis affecting the inner knee and demonstrated that at least one tested walking adjustment could reduce their joint loading. Its findings may not apply to people with advanced arthritis, other patterns of joint damage, or those whose knees respond differently.

Importantly, turning the toes inward or outward without professional assessment is not the same as receiving personalized gait retraining. An adjustment that helps one person might increase stress on another person's knee.
Larger trials, longer follow-up periods, and practical methods for delivering the treatment will be needed before clinicians can routinely prescribe it.

For now, the research points to an intriguing possibility: the way people walk may influence not only how much their knees hurt today, but potentially how well their cartilage holds up in the years ahead.

In April of 2025, Elgin Community College had six Flock safety cameras installed to “enhance the safety and security of students.” But by September of that year, the school’s administration grew concerned that Flock was sharing data with Customs and Border Patrol, that camera feeds were not properly secured, and that both law enforcement and the company’s employees were abusing access to the data.
A college in Illinois tried to cancel its Flock contact and it refused
Flock refused to take its cameras down so Elgin Community College covered them. The company snuck back to undo it.

So in October of 2025, Elgin Community College requested Flock to remove its cameras. According to Elgin’s President Peggy Heinrich, Flock rejected the request, saying it had not violated its contract. According to the Chicago Sun-Times, school officials reached out again in December, offered to pay for the remaining five months of the contract, and still requested that the cameras be removed. They were met with silence.

Heinrich said Elgin Community College staff began to cover the cameras using black trash bags and zip ties so that they would not be able to capture footage. But workers in an unmarked vehicle, which Heinrich assumed belonged to Flock, repeatedly removed the coverings.
“We were kind of in a back and forth for a bit where we’d cover, and then when they’d come to service, they’d remove,” Heinrich said. “Then we’d cover and then they’d remove.”
This continued until April of this year when the college’s contract expired, and Flock removed the cameras.

Welcome back to Power Play! Each week, senior writer Molly Taft tackles a topic around this midterm season’s biggest issue: data centers. If you’ve got a question or thought for the column, feel free to shoot Molly an email at [email protected] or reach them securely on Signal at mollytaft.76.

From surveillance and DOGE to Big Tech money and religious extremism, the midterms have never been more WIRED. Data centers are no exception: The public has rapidly turned on them since the beginning of the year.

The opposition is bipartisan, with many Republicans making a rare break from President Donald Trump. Candidates on both sides of the aisle are trying to attack their opponents for being pro–data center (or not anti–data center enough). I’ve spotted at least five candidates who have been given the derogatory “Data Center [Name]” moniker by their opponents, in an attempt to highlight their connections to the industry. (That includes two guys named Derek/Derrick getting this treatment.)

While polling shows that pocketbook issues are likely to be top of voters’ minds, data centers are a potent-enough issue that they could swing tight races—and ultimately tip the balance of power in Congress. Here are some of the races WIRED is keeping an eye on as we approach November 3.

The National Republican Senatorial Committee issued a memo in August warning that Democrat Sherrod Brown, running for Senate in Ohio, was hitting his opponent, Senator Jon Husted, so hard on data centers that it could tip the outcome of the race, calling it “a sleeper issue for the entire election cycle.” Brown has called Husted “the face of data centers in Ohio,” running ads that blame Husted for welcoming data centers to the state and driving energy bills up.

Senate Democrats have taken up Brown’s cause, torpedoing a bill sponsored by Husted and modeled after the White House’s ratepayer protection pledge, with Minority Leader Chuck Schumer calling the bill “toothless.”
Data centers have also seeped into many other toss-up Senate races, including in Michigan, Iowa, and Texas. But the Ohio race is still the top one to watch here.

All 435 seats in the House are up for grabs, and data centers have become flash points in dozens of races across the country. Among races labeled toss-ups by the Cook Political Report, I found numerous examples of candidates running data-center-related ads:

- In Michigan’s 7th district, Will Lawrence used local opposition to data centers to help win a tough Democratic primary. Lawrence is now facing off against Republican Tom Barrett and has aired several data-center-related ads, both attacking Barrett and advertising Lawrence’s promise to “stand up to corporate power.”

- In Pennsylvania’s 8th district, Republican incumbent Rob Bresnahan has run ads promising to be tough on the industry—despite holding data-center-related stocks and a previously friendly stance. His Democratic challenger, Paige Cognetti, has also run ads attacking the industry.

- In Ohio’s 9th, Democratic incumbent Marcy Kaptur has run ads railing against what she says is incumbent Derek Merrin’s history of giving tax breaks to data centers. (The ads call him “Data Center Derek.”) Merrin claims that Kaptur is misrepresenting his vote on a broader bill.

- In Wisconsin’s 3rd district, Democrat Rebecca Cooke has aired attack ads against incumbent Derrick van Orden’s history of taking contributions from data center developers, dubbing him “DC Derrick.” (Sound familiar?) Van Orden has also shot back by highlighting Cooke’s ties to the tech industry, claiming she is “responsible for covering up pristine Wisconsin farmland” with data centers.
- In New York’s 17th district, incumbent Republican Mike Lawler has aired an ad slamming Democratic opponent Cait Conley’s past statements that the Hudson Valley “needs” data centers.

At least 20 candidates in the 36 gubernatorial races have promised to enact some kind of data center moratorium if elected, according to research from Multistate. The only true hyperscale moratorium in place in the US right now was signed in July by New York governor Kathy Hochul, who holds a comfortable lead ahead of challenger Bruce Blakeman (who supports data center development).

Candidates without much daylight between them have still tried to gain the upper hand on the issue. In Wisconsin’s tight gubernatorial race, Republican Tom Tiffany has attacked Democrat David Crowley with ads calling him “Data Center David.” Both candidates say they support restrictions on the industry.

In states that have been hotbeds for data center activity, some candidates in tight races have been forced to pivot on the issue. Nowhere is this clearer than in Texas, where incumbent governor Greg Abbott has gone from welcoming data center development to putting a de facto moratorium on permits in less than a year. His opponent, Gina Hinojosa, says Abbott hasn’t gone far enough to regulate the industry.

Voters in eight states are looking at more than 30 local ballot measures around data centers. Once again, Ohio is a standout here: It’s responsible for more than half of those measures, from local moratoriums to referendums around rezoning.

WIRED science editor Brian Kahn and I got exclusive access to a startup that wants to pull water from the air using excess heat from data centers. While atmospheric water-harvesting technology has been around for a while, the startup has a unique spin. Atoco uses materials known as metal organic frameworks, or MOFs, which won one of its founders the Nobel Prize last year. The company’s previous prototypes have all needed to be hooked up to the grid to generate enough heat to extract water from the MOFs. The new version, though, only needs waste heat from industrial facilities—like data centers—to produce water, even in arid areas.
- In Memphis, Tennessee, home of Elon Musk’s SpaceX data centers, the city council postponed a vote on a data center moratorium. Business Insider has more on the “chaotic” meeting.

- Bloomberg reports that Oracle used trucks to ship in natural gas to a data center outside Salt Lake City to keep it online for more than a year—and is considering a similar move in New Mexico, where pipeline delays have held up a big project.

- As the midterms approach, environmental groups are flooding the zone with ads about the rush to build AI infrastructure powered by fossil fuels—just as Congress prepares to debate permitting reform. Heatmap has more.

Lockheed Martin on Friday unveiled PAC-3 Edge, a missile interceptor designed to defend against hypersonic and advanced missile threats, as the U.S. military looks to strengthen its capabilities to counter emerging aerial threats.

Growing demand for air and missile defense systems amid conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East has strained U.S. weapons stockpiles, prompting the U.S. Army to award Lockheed Martin a contract worth up to $58.6 billion in July to ramp up production of PAC-3 interceptors.

Lockheed Martin said PAC-3 Edge incorporates a new seeker, upgraded flight controls and a multi-pulse rocket motor supplied by Northrop Grumman, enhancing the interceptor’s ability to counter advanced threats, including hypersonic missiles, at longer ranges and higher altitudes.
