Just two weeks after it was launched, the Copernicus Sentinel-3C satellite returned its first images and measurements from two of its key instruments – a major milestone that confirms the satellite is working well and on the road to monitoring the health of Earth’s oceans, land, cryosphere and atmosphere.

This first set of images includes stunning views of Italy, the Arctic and the Caribbean from the satellite’s ocean and land colour instrument, as well as measurements of the height of the Greenland ice sheet and sea surface from its synthetic aperture radar altimeter.
Sentinel-3C is the third satellite in the Sentinel-3 series and will continue the mission’s long-term task of delivering environmental data that are essential for a wide range of applications.
As the workhorse mission for Copernicus, the Sentinel-3 satellites carry the same suite of instruments to measure systematically Earth’s oceans, land, cryosphere and atmosphere.

Over oceans, Sentinel-3 measures the temperature, colour and height of the sea surface as well as the thickness of sea ice to support, for example, the monitoring of marine pollution and marine heatwaves.

Over land, this innovative mission monitors drought and wildfires, maps the way land is used, checks vegetation health, and measures the height of rivers, lakes, and polar ice sheets as shown in the animation of Greenland below.
Sentinel-3's observations are also particularly valuable for providing near-realtime parameters for weather forecasting and for monitoring long-term changes associated with climate change.

The European Space Agency is still in the process of commissioning Sentinel-3C for service, an important and intricate task that will take another five months, but after only two weeks in orbit, the satellite’s initial images already showcase that it is on the road to excellence.

The first image, captured by the ocean and land colour instrument on 30 September, is a striking natural-colour view that reveals Italy in beautiful detail, stretching from southern Germany in the north to Sicily and the southern Mediterranean.

Just above the centre of the image, the broad, flat expanse of the Po Valley – Italy’s agricultural heartland – stands out in shades of brown and green. Just to the north, the snow-capped Alps form a dramatic contrast with the lowlands, their bright peaks clearly visible against the surrounding landscape. Across the rest of Italy, variations in green and brown reflect differences in vegetation, agriculture and other types of land cover.

To the east, the deep blue waters of the Adriatic Sea separate Italy from the Balkan Peninsula, which is partially visible in the image. Noticeable variations in sea colour can be seen along Italy’s eastern coastline, where lighter blue waters hug the shore. These brighter tones are likely caused by sediment carried into the sea by rivers and transported along the coast.

On Italy’s western side, the dark waters of the Tyrrhenian Sea surround the islands of Sardinia and Sicily, which are clearly visible, while Corsica is largely obscured by cloud. Together, the contrasting colours of the land, snow-covered mountains and surrounding seas provide a vivid view of Italy’s diverse landscape from space.

The second image, also captured by the ocean and land colour instrument on 30 September, features part of the Canadian Arctic Archipelago, to the west of Greenland. Snow- and ice-covered islands dominate the scene, with rugged coastlines, deep fjords and exposed rock creating intricate patterns. At this time of the year sea ice is at a minimum but some fractured floes are visible on the dark open water.

The Arctic is warming much faster than the global average, causing rapid melting of ice on land and ice in the sea, which leads to further warming through feedback loops. Sentinel-3’s different instruments measure ice in different ways – all contributing to a better understanding of the vulnerable polar regions.

The third image captured on 29 September, also by the ocean and land colour instrument, is a spectacular view of part of the Caribbean, with Cuba to the south and the Bahamas towards the top of the image. Shallow waters around the islands appear in a beautiful turquoise set against the darker deeper waters of the open sea.

Low-lying islands and coastal regions around the world are at risk of sea-level rise. Sentinel-3’s synthetic aperture radar altimeter measures changes in the height of the sea surface to help monitor rising seas and contribute to action on climate change and mitigation strategies.

The map above shows measurements of sea-surface height across the Atlantic Ocean and Mediterranean Sea from Sentinel-3C’s synthetic aperture radar altimeter, compared to the Copernicus Marine Service multimission sea-level anomaly. These new data demonstrate that the altimeter is performing well and comparable to current measurements. Once commissioned, the altimeter will contribute to monitoring changes in sea-surface height around the world, complementing long-term records from missions such as Copernicus Sentinel-6 and Jason.
High-precision satellite altimetry has enabled scientists to establish the rate of global sea-level rise, which has averaged 3.64 mm per year since 1999, with the rate of rise accelerating.
The altimeter will also measure changes in the height of lakes, rivers, sea ice and land ice, also complementing the upcoming Copernicus CRISTAL mission.

The animation above shows measurements of the height of the Greenland Ice Sheet acquired by Sentinel-3C between 30 September and 4 October. The measurements also demonstrate that the altimeter is performing well, with all of the measurement tracks closely matching the reference digital elevation model.

Monitoring changes in the height of the Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets is essential for understanding the impacts of climate change and, importantly, for improving predictions of future sea-level rise. Ice loss from the sheets is a major contributor to sea-level rise, and satellite altimetry provides a valuable way of tracking changes in their surface elevation over time.

All in all, these first acquisitions from Sentinel-3C’s ocean and land colour instrument and from its synthetic aperture radar altimeter provide early confirmation of the satellite’s performance and mark an important step towards full operational service following the completion of the commissioning phase.
Coming soon: the first observations from Sentinel-3C’s sea and land surface temperature radiometer – stay tuned.

Sentinel-3 is part of Copernicus – the Earth observation component of the EU’s Space programme. For the Sentinel-3 satellites, ESA is responsible for the development and implementation of the satellites as well as the operations up to the completion of commissioning. After the commissioning phase, the Sentinel-3 mission is jointly managed by ESA and Eumetsat, where Eumetsat is responsible for routine satellite operations and the delivery of marine and atmospheric data, while ESA delivers land, cryosphere, inland water and offline atmospheric products. Together, the two agencies provide mission data for the Copernicus services and users worldwide.

From soft peeps to piercing calls, birds produce a wide range of sounds. But scientists recently discovered that two South American species take their calls to ear-splitting extremes, making deafening vocalizations on par with a jackhammer.

The bare-throated bellbird and the red-legged seriema can produce sounds at amplitudes that exceed 120 decibels, according to a study published September 29 in the journal Evolution. They’re now among the ranks of the white bellbird, another South American species, for the loudest known birds on the planet.

Researchers behind the new work didn’t specifically set out to find the world’s noisiest birds. Rather, they wanted to take advantage of recent technological advancements that have made it easier to measure vocal amplitude, the height of a sound wave and a key element of loudness.

“Until recently, it was very impractical to go out into the field and measure amplitude,” lead author João Menezes, an evolutionary biologist who conducted the research while at the University of Massachusetts Amherst, tells the New York Times’ Taylor Mitchell Brown. “It’s kind of stepping into a whole new world.”

The researchers started the project in Amherst, Massachusetts, during the Covid-19 lockdowns, when the unusually quiet circumstances made it easier to isolate and record bird song. They used a laser rangefinder to measure their distance from a specific bird, as well as a sound level meter, which allowed them to isolate that bird’s call from other noises.

“Even recording from my window or from the backyard, almost always that would be [the amplitude of] a new species,” Menezes tells the Washington Post’s Meghan Bartels. “It’s not often that you get to do this kind of exploratory science where you just go out into the field and document things for the first time, especially with birds.”

From Massachusetts, they headed next to Brazil, where they recorded birds in several different habitats. The scientists ultimately collected amplitude data on 123 bird species between December 2018 and January 2025, filling a major gap in scientists’ understanding of how loud birds can sing. Previously, scientists only had amplitude data for ten of those species—even the ubiquitous Canada goose had never been measured.

“We’ve been able to vastly increase the number of species for which there is amplitude data,” study co-author Jeffrey Podos, also an evolutionary biologist at the University of Massachusetts Amherst, says in a statement. “This is basic, foundational research that no one else has managed to do on this scale.”

Their amplitude database captures the impressive range of bird vocalization volumes. At the low end, they documented the dusky-throated hermit, a hummingbird that buzzes at a modest 64 decibels, about the same volume as a normal conversation. At the high end, the bare-throated bellbird and red-legged seriema are both about as loud as a trumpeting elephant or a chainsaw.

Comparing the amplitude data with the birds’ anatomy revealed that species with bigger bodies and wider mouth openings also tended to be the loudest. This is probably because “bigger birds have bulkier muscles, which are capable of creating greater internal pressures, which ultimately generate louder sounds, and then broader mouths allow more energy to radiate into the environment,” Menezes tells CNN’s Amarachi Orie.

Still, the researchers have many unanswered questions. The big one: Why are some birds so much louder than others? The researchers hypothesized that the loudest birds evolved their high-volume calls to attract numerous mates, or to communicate through dense vegetation. But those explanations don’t hold up for the red-legged seriema, so there must be some other factor driving the evolution of its loud vocalizations.

“The seriema is the opposite of those two things,” Menezes tells WBUR’s Barbara Moran. “It’s a super open-habitat bird, like pasture, and it’s strictly monogamous. So, it forms a pair for the breeding season, and that’s it.”

There’s no single answer to the question of which species holds the title of “world’s loudest bird”—it depends on how researchers define loudness. The bare-throated bellbird, for example, produced the loudest individual call, reaching nearly 131 decibels, per CNN. But when researchers averaged the loudest calls across individual birds, the red-legged seriema came out on top at nearly 121 decibels. Averaging the vocalizations’ peak volumes, on the other hand, allowed the white bellbird to take the lead at 127 decibels.

Scientists are still unraveling the evolutionary underpinnings of super loud birdsong. But in the meantime, their work could have important implications for conservation. For example, reliable amplitude data could help researchers use audio recordings to determine not just whether a species is present, but also how close those birds might be and how many individuals are nearby, Connor Wood, an ornithologist at Cornell University who wasn’t involved in the study, tells the Washington Post.
The findings could also help scientists better understand how birds may adapt to a changing world.

“Amplitude is so critical to the ability of birds to communicate with each other, that it is really important for us to understand exactly how that might be able to change,” Nathan Senner, an ornithologist at the University of Massachusetts Amherst who also wasn’t involved with the study, tells WBUR. “How they evolve is really fundamental to our understanding of how they might continue to evolve as our world changes.”

Historians have long known that Lismore, a small isle in the Inner Hebrides of Scotland, was home to a medieval monastery called Lios Mòr. Written records detail its sixth-century founding by St. Mo Luóc, one of the early monks who spread Christianity to northern Britain. But with very little archaeological evidence, apart from a broken granite cross, scholars could not confirm Lios Mòr’s size, style or significance—until now.

According to an article published in the journal Antiquity last week, a group of local volunteers led by archaeologist Clare Ellis, of the firm Argyll Archaeology, discovered an early medieval cemetery, various structures and “sophisticated craftworking of international importance” during excavations near Lismore’s 13th-century parish church.

“For centuries, Lismore’s early monastery was known mainly from written records and local tradition,” study co-author Gordon Noble, an archaeologist at the University of Aberdeen, says in a statement. “We can now see that it was a thriving center of worship, craftsmanship and learning, whose importance may have rivaled some of the best-known monasteries in early medieval Britain.”

Lismore’s historical society began searching for the site of Mo Luóc’s monastery in 2016. A “dynamic minority” of the island’s 170 or so residents crowdfunded and ran the digs, Robert Hay, a retired local scientist and dig participant, tells the Guardian’s Esther Addley. Grants, donations and yet more crowdfunding enabled the enthusiastic locals to hire Ellis to lead excavations near the site of Lismore’s 13th-century church, which still holds services.

“The research aimed to determine whether the site of the later medieval cathedral at Lismore was also the location of Mo Luóc’s early monastery, and to assess the scale, nature and status of the settlement,” Ellis says in the statement.

The dig uncovered a medieval cemetery containing at least six burials radiocarbon dated to between 650 and 1040 C.E. The archaeologists also unearthed a piece of an “early medieval cross slab,” per the study. In another area, they found more human remains and additional fragments of carved stone crosses.

“This was clearly a really important early Christian establishment,” Noble tells the Guardian. He compares it to Scotland’s famed Iona monastery, which was founded in 563 C.E. Both settlements were products of a medieval missionary movement that aimed to spread Christianity throughout pagan Britain. The monks succeeded. By the seventh century, Britain was Christianized.

Elsewhere on the cathedral property, researchers found the remains of an oval-shaped building paved with a layer of limestone. Dated to between the seventh and tenth centuries, it contained remnants of craftwork, handmade pottery, struck flint and an antler.

Another trench boasted extensive evidence of precious metalwork: more than 1,000 pieces of debris, including well-preserved molds and crucibles once used to melt down and cast gold, copper and silver. Hay describes them as “the best small crucibles ever found in Scotland,” per the Guardian.

Clay molds and crucibles are “unusual” finds for a monastic site, Noble tells Scientific American’s Jackie Flynn Mogensen. “It’s one of the largest metalworking assemblages we have from any site, secular or sacred, in this time period,” he adds.

The Lismore monastery appears to have an unusually large footprint. This, coupled with evidence of precious metals and craftsmanship, suggests the community was actually considerably wealthy and “far more than a small island church,” per the statement.
As Noble says to Scientific American, Lios Mòr appears to have been “a very significant mover and shaker” in its day. “It’ll be really exciting to see what shows up in the coming years.”
In September, the Antarctic ozone hole peaked at 10.6 million square miles—the second largest ever observed for this time of year.

Using data from the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service, scientists found that the ozone hole started growing earlier than usual in August. By September 20, it reached a size close to its October 2015 peak, when it was 10.8 million square miles.

To understand what’s happening, we first need to understand the ozone layer. The ozone layer lies in the Earth’s stratosphere and protects our planet from harmful ultraviolet (UV) radiation that can harm humans, plants and animals. The infamous ozone hole is actually a patch of depleted ozone in the stratosphere over Antarctica that is mainly caused by chemicals called chlorofluorocarbons, or CFCs. While the 1987 Montreal Protocol phased out the use of CFCs globally, they can persist in the atmosphere for decades.

The ozone hole’s size fluctuates every year. For about three months each fall—the Southern Hemisphere’s spring—the hole opens inside the stratospheric polar vortex, a large band of fast-spinning westerly winds that encircles Antarctica and the Southern Ocean. The vortex traps freezing air inside and leads to the formation of polar stratospheric clouds, writes a New Zealand-based research team in The Conversation. “Chemical reactions on particles in this rare type of cloud then activate ozone-depleting gases,” they add.

This year brought a stronger and colder polar vortex. “We have unusually strong winds and cold temperatures over the pole that have created the conditions possible for the hole to grow to the size it has today,” research team member Hannah Kessenich, a physicist at the University of Otago in New Zealand, tells the Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC News). By late January, the hole will shrink again.
Did you know? Wildfires can destroy the ozone layer

- Climate change has increased the frequency of wildfires, which is not a good thing when it comes to mending the ozone layer. A study published in Nature in 2023 found that particles in wildfire smoke spark chemical reactions in the atmosphere that break down ozone.

So, should we be worried? “This year’s ozone hole shouldn’t be a cause for alarm,” Kessenich told Live Science's Sascha Pare in an email. “However, there are still many unanswered questions. It’s something we need to keep a close eye on.”

Kessenich and other experts underscore the fact that the ozone hole size we’re currently seeing isn’t a sign that the Montreal Protocol isn’t working. “We look at the depth of the hole rather than the area to assess how we’re coming along in terms of the recovery from those chemicals,” Kessenich says to ABC News.

In fact, this year’s hole isn’t as deep as it has been in previous years, and year-to-year variability is to be expected. “We have to look at the longer term trends, and those metrics continue to tell us that the ozone hole is slowly recovering as expected,” adds Susan Solomon, an atmospheric chemist at MIT, in an email to Live Science.

There will, however, be impacts on weather across the Southern Hemisphere. A larger ozone hole shifts the Southern Annular Mode into a positive phase, which affects winds and precipitation in different areas. In Australia, for example, it causes increased rainfall on the country’s southeast coast, Kessenich and her colleagues write in The Conversation.

Researchers are still trying to understand how climate change impacts the strength of the polar vortex, and why bigger ozone holes are persisting longer than they used to. It could be that changes in global atmospheric dynamics are making longer-lived ozone holes more likely, which in turn could mean our timelines for ozone recovery need to be adapted.
“It's too soon to tell what has been driving dynamical variability in recent years, but more research is needed,” Kessenich says to Live Science.

NEW YORK, Oct. 10 (UPI) -- The Walking Dead legends Norman Reedus and Melissa McBride appeared at New York Comic Con Friday to talk about their 15-year journey as zombie-apocalypse survivors Daryl and Carol.
The stars played the best friends for 11 seasons of the flagship TWD series, which took place in the American southwest, and for four seasons of the European spin-off, Daryl Dixon.
Season 4 has already been filmed and premieres in February. The final season is being billed as "one last journey, one last fight."
"It was super-weird, the whole last week [of filming,]" Reedus, 57, told UPI at a New York Comic Con press conference Friday.

"Not to give spoilers away in any way, whatsoever. But it was sad. It was an accomplishment. It felt like that quote from David Bowie, when they say, 'What do you think your last words are going to be when you die?' And he goes, 'But, but, but...' It was a little bit like that," the actor recalled.

"But it felt like an accomplishment. It felt like we told the story we were trying to tell and it was sad for the crew, too. You become this really big family, especially when we're going overseas and hanging around new people in a new place and it was very emotional all the way."

"There were three things: there was Melissa's last scene and there was Norman's last scene and there's the last scene they did together," executive producer David Zabel said. "So, there's sort of three things, each of which was emotionally different."
McBride added, "And Norman's last scene was the last shot we ever shot as a show."
Zabel said that just because this chapter of The Walking Dead is over, doesn't mean there aren't still stories in this universe to tell.
"There will still be shows," executive producer Scott M. Gimple said. "See what's in them."
Oct. 10 (UPI) -- Christa Pike, who survived a botched execution attempt, was released from the hospital Saturday, 10 days later.
She was transferred back to the prison in Nashville where she was held before her execution.

"Christa Pike was discharged from a local hospital and is now at Deborah K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center where she has been housed for more than 30 years," her attorneys, Stephen Ferrell, Luke Ihnen, Randy Spivey and Kelly Gleason, said in a statement Saturday. "She is grateful to the first responders and her medical team for their care in these extraordinary circumstances. She is continuing to receive medical care at the prison, and we will continue to track her recovery."
Pike, 50, was the first woman Tennessee tried to execute in more than 200 years on Sept. 30. She received two doses of pentobarbital, each of which could have been lethal.

Pike survived the injections and was seen by witnesses snoring and breathing. She was taken to the hospital in critical condition and unconscious. Her lawyers had believed she was brain dead, but she woke up and began speaking on Oct. 6. On Thursday, her lawyer said she was up and walking in the hospital.
According to the Death Penalty Information Center, Pike is the only person known to have survived an execution attempt after getting a lethal injection in the United States.

Pike, along with her then-boyfriend and another young woman, tortured and killed Colleen Slemmer, 19, in 1995. Pike, who was 18, is the only one of the three with a death sentence. The boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, was ineligible for the death penalty because he was 17. The other woman, Shadolla Peterson, testified against Pike and Shipp and was given probation.
Oct. 9 (UPI) -- Hurricane Isaias landed near Destin, Fla., Friday evening, and was downgraded to a post-tropical cyclone, bringing high winds, rain and flooding.
One person in Escambia County, Fla., died "due to a downed tree," county officials said, and another was killed in Birmingham, Ala. Both were killed when trees fell on homes.
Across the southeastern United States, about 860,000 people were without power Saturday, with trees and power lines down.
Emergency management in Santa Rosa County, Fla., situated between Pensacola and Destin, said the majority of roads in the county are "impassable due to down trees and/or power lines."
More than 80% of customers were without power, and wind gusts rose to more than 100 mph Friday night.
Thirty teams from the Florida Department of Transportation are assessing damage Saturday in the Panhandle.

"At first light, thousands of linemen and utility crews have convoyed from Sandestin and along the I-10 corridor to get to work, focusing on outages in the hardest hit communities," Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said.
"It was pitch black out. The storm had passed. It was safe enough to go out, and they were doing it," he added.
Some airports in the area have reopened. Northwest Florida Beaches Airport reopened to commercial service, but the Destin, Fort Walton Beach and Pensacola airports are still closed.

Heavy rainfall will move quickly into the Tennessee Valley and southern Appalachians. Flash flooding and landslides are possible, especially in mountainous areas, the National Hurricane Center said in its 4 a.m. CDT Saturday update.
Isaias was about 105 miles south of Birmingham, Ala., and about 25 miles south-southeast of Mobile, with maximum sustained winds of about 35 mph. There are no more weather warnings in effect.
Isaias is the first hurricane of the year in the Atlantic basin, despite a strong El Niño.
Through the weekend, Isaias is expected to bring 4 to 8 inches of rainfall across southern Alabama, the Florida Panhandle, the Big Bend region and southwest Georgia.
Localized totals up to 15 inches were also possible across the Panhandle and Big Bend.
Forecasters expected the coastal Carolinas to receive 2 to 5 inches of rain, with localized totals up to 10 inches also possible.
The remainder of the Southeast was forecast to get 2 to 5 inches. A risk for tornadoes will persist through Saturday afternoon across parts of the eastern Panhandle, Georgia and the Carolinas.
Wind shear in the Atlantic has kept hurricanes at bay so far this season, but low wind shear in the Gulf helped Isaias.

Noordwijk, the Netherlands | September 22, 2026 – During the international Industry Space Days 2026 event at the European Space Agency’s ESTEC facility in Noordwijk, the Netherlands, the Latvian Mobile Telephone (LMT) Group and the globally leading space consultancy Novaspace signed a cooperation agreement on the development of a concept for telecommunications innovation platform for Latvia to link the national connectivity sector with the international satellite industry. The initiative follows the successful ESA 5G/6G Non-Terrestrial Network Hub model and will explore Latvia’s potential role within this network.

Signing the agreement marks a pivotal step toward creating a hub for developing an internationally competitive telecommunications sector in Latvia. The hub will strategically bring LMT into the space industry and impact the emergence of a wider Latvia’s space innovation ecosystem in next-generation satellite technologies, products, and services tailored to commercial applications, resilient critical infrastructure, security, digitalization and green transition. Essentially, the hub will attract national and international cooperation, funding and talent.

The next generation of mobile communications is closely linked to the rapid growth of the space economy globally. The space infrastructure is already gradually enhancing terrestrial networks, and the 6G era of telecommunications will seamlessly link terrestrial and non-terrestrial networks. The rationale for such development is efficient and resilient connectivity, especially essential in scenarios involving severe weather, power outages or physical infrastructure disruptions.

This initiative builds upon LMT Group’s strategic expansion of its track record in connectivity innovation. LMT is already collaborating with ESA and satellite operator Sateliot to pioneer energy efficient dual-mode satellite Internet of Things (IoT) connectivity, enabled by Latvia’s associate membership in ESA. The hardware and software to be developed will cover the current market gap in devices that can seamlessly switch between terrestrial and satellite networks. The planned 5G/6G NTN hub is a natural next step in scaling LMT’s technological footprint within Europe’s space ecosystem.

“LMT has long evolved beyond traditional mobile operations into a full-scale technology innovator. As we prepare for the 6G era, integrating satellite communications into our infrastructure and service portfolio is essential. Our goal is to ensure resilient, secure communications for new commercial services and for critical infrastructure under any circumstances, to produce exportable space technologies and develop services that contribute to digitalization and green transition. Partnering with Novaspace will allow us to define Latvia’s unique value proposition within the European space ecosystem and expand local high-tech expertise,” Ingmārs Pūķis, VP & Member of the Management Board at LMT.

The agreement was signed under the EU-funded FIERCE Ecosystem Building Programme, in which LMT participates as an innovation intermediary and Novaspace provides strategic support and space-market expertise. Through the programme, Novaspace will work directly with LMT to define and validate the concept, guiding LMT towards a Latvian 5G/6G terrestrial and non-terrestrial network (TN/NTN) hub. The joint effort will focus on identifying Latvia’s distinctive regional value proposition and connecting the future hub with the wider European 5G/6G and NTN ecosystem, rather than replicating existing European initiatives.

“At Novaspace, we are delighted to partner with LMT Group through the FIERCE project. The strength of Europe’s space sector depends on active participation across all Member States, and Latvia is well positioned both to benefit from and contribute to Europe’s growing space economy. Flagship European programmes such as Copernicus, Galileo, EGNOS and IRIS² are creating new opportunities for innovation, resilient connectivity and commercial growth. Drawing on Novaspace’s global market expertise, we look forward to supporting LMT in defining a distinctive role for Latvia within Europe’s 5G/6G and non-terrestrial network ecosystem,” Gabrielle Brophy, Senior Manager at Novaspace.

The planned hub will be developed together with research and industry partners in the region. This collaborative framework will help retain and grow specialized engineering and scientific competencies in the Baltic region.

The signing ceremony in Noordwijk was attended by representatives of the European Space Agency, Novaspace, the Latvian embassy in the Netherlands, the Ministry of Education and Science of the Republic of Latvia, the Investment and Development Agency of Latvia, Novaspace in representation of the FIERCE project and LMT.

DURANGO, Colo., Oct. 5, 2026 — Agile Space Industries today announced that Jonathan Baliff has joined its Board of Directors, bringing extensive experience in aerospace, finance, and corporate leadership. His appointment, alongside the addition of Theo Squires as Director of Strategy & Corporate Development, strengthens Agile’s ability to execute its long-term growth strategy, support capital formation, and pursue strategic opportunities as the company continues to scale.

Agile is entering its next phase with growing opportunities across the commercial and national security space. In particular, the company’s recent selection for the SpaceWERX Strategic Funding Increase (STRATFI) program reflects support for adding the ability to supply complete propulsion subsystems. As Agile expands its capabilities and production capacity, the company is also strengthening the financial and strategic foundation needed to support its long-term objectives.

“Agile has built significant momentum, and our next phase of growth requires the financial capability and oversight to match our technical expertise,” said Chris Pearson, CEO of Agile Space Industries. “Jonathan’s experience in aerospace, capital formation and corporate transformation, combined with Theo’s focus on strategy and corporate development, will help us evaluate new opportunities, make strategic investments and position Agile for sustainable, long-term growth.”
Jonathan Baliff Joins Board of Directors

Baliff brings extensive experience across aerospace, finance, and corporate leadership. A former U.S. Air Force aviator and engineer, he currently serves as an operating partner at Genesis Park, where he played a central role in the formation and financing of Redwire Corporation and later served as its chief financial officer. He previously served as president and CEO of Bristow Group and held senior leadership positions at NRG Energy and Credit Suisse. His experience raising capital, guiding strategic investments, and leading organizations through periods of growth and transformation will support Agile as the company continues to scale.

“Agile has proven it has the technology and operational expertise to compete, win, and profitably grow in a rapidly evolving space market,” said Baliff. “Our customers and capital providers will partner with us as we scale Agile’s technology, expand capacity, and efficiently deploy capital to support the company’s growth. Expanding Corporate Development to Support Long-Term Strategy

Squires serves as Agile’s Director of Strategy & Corporate Development. Before joining Agile, he served as an intelligence officer in the Royal Australian Navy, where his work included a bilateral space program involving the United States and Australia. He also worked at Boston Consulting Group, advising advanced manufacturing companies on strategy and operations. At Agile, his experience supports capital formation, strategic investments and potential acquisitions of complementary technologies and capabilities to support the company’s broader growth strategy.

“Scaling advanced propulsion hardware requires both technical innovation and a disciplined approach to capital investment,” said Squires. “Our focus is on building a financial foundation to support higher-rate production while identifying strategic opportunities that complement Agile’s existing capabilities. During his board service, Rubin contributed valuable legal expertise and counsel as Agile navigated a period of significant growth. The company is grateful for his contributions and looks forward to continuing to benefit from his experience and institutional knowledge in his advisory role.

Ukraine: UN condemns latest attacks and calls for civilian protection

The UN Humanitarian Coordinator for Ukraine on Wednesday called for an end to attacks against civilians following further overnight strikes by Russian forces that reportedly killed at least 19 in the Chernihiv Region.
Among the dead in Pryluky were five children, three of them babies, according to the latest information from local authorities. One of the children died along with his mother and grandmother.
At least 50 others were reportedly injured when residential buildings were struck. The casualty toll is expected to rise as rescue operations continue.
The overnight wave of attacks also reportedly killed around 25 others and injured dozens of civilians in Kremenchuk in the Poltava region, Kyiv and Oleksandriia in the Kirovohrad region.
According to the latest data, 15,280 civilians were killed or injured in Ukraine during the first eight months of this year.

“Families must never live through the horror of seeing their children placed in constant danger or buried under the rubble of their own homes. This pattern of increasing harm to civilians must end,” the UN’s top official in the country Matthias Schmale said in a statement.
On 5 and 6 October, airstrikes hit a hospital in Kryvyi Rih and ambulances in Kramatorsk, injuring health workers.
Ukrainian Red Cross workers were also injured while travelling to assist people affected by an attack in Zaporizhzhia.
“Civilians, including children, homes and essential civilian infrastructure are protected under international humanitarian law,” Mr. Schmale reiterated.

Briefing journalists in New York Wednesday, UN Spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric said the Secretary-General strongly condemned the ongoing attacks. He also expressed deep concern over the rising number of civilian casualties.
“All attacks targeting civilians and civilian infrastructure, wherever they occur, are a violation of international humanitarian law and must end immediately,” Mr. Dujarric said.
Humanitarian teams in Ukraine reported that attacks and frontline hostilities over the previous 24 hours had caused more than 150 civilian casualties.

During the first eight months of this year, the UN and its humanitarian partners assisted 1.5 million people affected by strikes across Ukraine, as attacks continue to intensify and spread to areas farther from the front lines.
UN rights chief: Legacy of slavery and colonialism is still fuelling racism

The legacy of enslavement and colonialism continues to shape the lives of Africans and people of African descent, UN human rights chief Volker Türk said on Thursday, calling for urgent action to deliver reparatory justice beyond financial compensation.
Over 30 million people were violently uprooted from Africa and condemned to a life of slavery.
Yet no country involved in enslavement or colonialism has fully confronted this past.

Speaking at a high-level dialogue on reparatory Justice in Geneva, Mr. Türk said the transatlantic trade was an organised system of domination that treated tens of millions of African men, women and children as commodities.
Women and girls suffered particularly grave abuses, including sexual and gender-based violence, he underscored.

Reiterating that the legacy of these injustices lives on today, Mr. Türk told delegates that “their consequences – together with those of colonialism more generally – continue to shape who has opportunity, security, and power – and who does not.”

Calls for reparatory justice have been growing, said High Commissioner Türk. Some States, universities, religious groups and businesses have begun to confront their historic role in African enslavement.
Racism can be encountered in everyday life, from employment and housing to education and healthcare, the UN rights chief said.

In some regions, police are several times more likely to use force against people of African descent, while people of the dispora are also disproportionately represented in prisons and criminal justice systems.
Mr. Türk also warned that emerging technologies could compound existing inequalities.

“Artificial intelligence and other technologies are already reproducing human biases,” he said. “If we are not careful, they could deepen systemic racism against Africans and people of African descent.”
Mr. Türk stressed that reparatory justice should not be understood as financial compensation alone.

Instead, it should include confronting the truth about the past, formal apologies, truth-seeking initiatives and memorials recognising the experiences and contributions of Africans and people of African descent.
Other measures can include the restitution of cultural artefacts, compensation, education and awareness-raising, as well as medical and psychosocial support to address intergenerational trauma.
The UN rights office (OHCHR) has developed a series of explainers to help States advance reparatory justice, highlighting key measures and examples of action, including apologies.

“No State has fully accounted for the harms of the past or systemic racism today,” he continued noting that many countries still lack anti-racism legislation and that fewer than one in four have comprehensive anti-discrimination laws.

Calling for stronger implementation of existing laws and targeted investment to remove barriers affecting access to healthcare, housing, education, justice and employment, he said that Africans and people of African descent, particularly women, must be at the centre of reparatory efforts.

Mr. Türk urged reforms to the international financial architecture, including measures to ease unsustainable debt and strengthen the participation of African countries in international decision-making.
“A child born in 2026 should not have to carry the weight of centuries of racial discrimination and the horrors of the past,” he concluded.
Former UN human rights chief Navi Pillay awarded Nobel Peace Prize
She was honoured “for her efforts to promote peace and international law”, the Norwegian Nobel Committee said in a statement.

The committee said the award was going “to a person who with exceptional courage and integrity has led the way towards a more comprehensive global legal order,” noting that she “has been instrumental in ensuring that war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide are prosecuted.”

Ms. Pillay served as the UN human rights chief from September 2008 through August 2014, but her career has spanned more than 50 years - from fighting apartheid in her homeland to defending civilians in conflict zones.

She is a former chair of the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory and was appointed a judge at the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda (ICTR) and the International Criminal Court (ICC) in the Hague, in addition to serving as an ad hoc judge with the International Court of Justice (ICJ), the UN's highest court.

“A common thread runs from her early work defending Nelson Mandela and others who stood up against apartheid to her service as a judge in some of the key international court cases of our time,” the Nobel Committee said.
An ‘independent voice of justice’: Guterres

In a statement congratulating the new Nobel laureate, UN Secretary-General António Guterres said Ms. Pillay has shown “that the force of law must prevail over the law of force and that defending human rights is the surest safeguard against injustice.”

He hailed her as “a champion of international law and human rights, and a steadfast, independent voice of justice”, adding that “in its citation, the Nobel Committee reminded the world that peace must be built on lasting principles, not the will of the powerful."
Navanethem “Navi” Pillay was born in South Africa in 1941 to a Tamil Indian family and was the first non-white woman to establish a legal practice in the country.
As a lawyer, she acted as a defence attorney for anti-apartheid activists, exposing torture, and helping to establish key rights for prisoners on notorious Robben Island.

In her role as chair of the Independent International Commission, which is appointed by the UN Human Rights Council, she oversaw its 2025 report that said Israel’s actions in the Gaza Strip constituted genocide.

On receiving the news of Ms. Pillay's honour, the current UN human rights chief, Volker Türk, warmly congratulated the woman he described as a big sister.

“To say it is well deserved is a total understatement, and especially at a time when human rights are under attack on so many fronts, including from those who wield enormous power, this award is particularly poignant,” he said, speaking in Geneva.
“It is an award to all those who around the world dedicate their lives to the defense of human rights, often at great risk to their security.”
Moreover, it is “a recognition, a reaffirmation, that human rights, the rule of law and justice and accountability are fundamental to everything - to peace, to security and prosperity,” he added.
In an October 2025 interview with UN News in Geneva, Ms. Pillay reflected on her lifetime of fighting for human rights, justice and equality.

“I didn't think apartheid would end in my lifetime,” she recalled. “So, what happened? We had the collective support of people all over the world, even children. If we can achieve that, we can have a better human rights protection system.”

Her experience in the anti-apartheid struggle shaped her belief in international solidarity, which she carried into her role as a judge and president of the ITCR, which prosecuted persons responsible for the 1994 genocide in Rwanda.
During her eight years there, she helped establish groundbreaking legal precedents in the fight against genocide and gender-based violence.
As UN human rights chief, Ms. Pillay continued to champion the participation of civil society and victims’ voices in shaping global human rights standards.

“When the UN started, it was just a club for the States,” she told UN News. “Everything we have today for human rights protection didn’t happen just because the States woke up one day. It comes from the pressure of civil society. That’s why I value these institutions.”
